units.text: DIRAC: Data Production Management
Introduction

DIRAC is LHCb's combined Grid Workload and Data Management System [1] providing the functionalities to support the LHCb Computing Model [2]. Built on a common framework [3], the Workload and Data Management Systems are able to coordinate their activity to provide data-driven production management. It is 'data-driven' because as data becomes available an action on that data is automatically performed. A data file can be automatically replicated when it is created, which in turn spawns a job to process the file, which in turn can trigger the replication of the job output. This chain can be long or short, contain transfer or processing steps, extended or shortened, to meet the requirement of the dataflow.
LHCb Computing Model

The LHCb Computing Model describes the dataflow model for all stages of processing for real and simulated data. It also defines the role of the Tier-0, Tier-1 and Tier-2 computing centers (as seen in Figure 1).

The RAW data generated at the LHCb detector is uploaded to Grid enabled mass storage at CERN, as the Tier-0 center CERN takes archival responsibility for this data. To ensure data persistency each RAW file is replicated to an external Tier-1 center mass storage system to create a distributed replica of the entire RAW dataset. This RAW data is then processed  (reconstructed and stripped [2]) at the Tier-1 centers (including CERN) according to pledged computing resources. The output of processing is DST files which are used by physicists for analysis. To ensure high data availability for analysis DST files are replicated to all Tier-1 centers. Simulation data is generated at the Tier2 sites and their data uploaded to the associated Tier-1 center (including CERN) where the processing is executed.

As the generation center CERN takes the role of a Tier-0 center and maintains the master copies of all RAW data. In the model CERN has a dual role and for processing activities it is considered as a Tier-1 center. The 7 LHCb Tier-1 centers (CERN, CNAF, FZK, IN2P3, NIKHEF, PIC, RAL) provide computing resources for the reconstruction, stripping and user analysis and storage resources for the processing output and RAW data. Each site provides resources to store all DST files for distributed analysis activities.
LHCb Data Upload To The Grid

The LHCb High Level Trigger (HLT) will write 2GB RAW physics data files to the Online Storage System approximately every 30 seconds. For each file an entry is made in the Online Run Database (RunDB) which manages file states and access [4]. These files are replicated to CASTOR [5] storage at CERN and persisted on the local buffer until integrity of the CASTOR file is ensured.
Replication and Performance

The RunDB manages the file state machine within the Online system and triggers the replication to CASTOR by placing a request to the DIRAC RequestDB (see Figure 2). The DIRAC RequestDB and associated agents are deployed on gateway machines with access to the Online Storage and private Gb network to the CERN IT fabric. The requests are persisted in the RequestDB, retrieved and executed by 'Transfer Agents'. In case of failures the requests retried until success. The agents use CASTOR's proprietary RFIO protocol to transfer to dedicated disk pools.

A series of performance studies have been conducted to determine optimal configuration for the deployment of the DIRAC services and components. A single DIRAC instance was deployed on a single gateway machine and the number of agents executing replication requests was varied. Each configuration was deployed for 24 hours and the read rate from the Online storage system was monitored at intervals of 2 seconds. The mean read rate from the disk pools increased with the number of clients until network saturation, approaching the 1Gb/s limit, occurred with four clients (see Figure 3). With DIRAC instances deployed on two gateway machines, each with four agents executing requests, it was possible to saturate two dedicated 1Gb/s network connections  Figure 2. Architecture for Ensuring RAW Data Integrity (see Figure 4). These rates are well within the observed capability of the Online storage [6] and in excess of the 200MB/s peak rate desired by LHCb.
Ensuring Data Integrity

Once the replication to CASTOR is complete, the integrity of the file must be verified. Whilst migrating a file to tape CASTOR calculates the Adler32 checksum which is also calculated at the original write time at the Online storage. If the two checksums match the integrity of the file in CASTOR can be assumed. The RunDB can then be instructed that the file is a candidate for removal from the Online SAN. The DIRAC architecture for this procedure is shown in Figure  2. Once replication of a file completes it is registered in the 'Online Integrity Service' which maintains a list of files awaiting migration to tape. A further agent retrieves this list and contacts  CASTOR to retrieve the checksum. If the file was migrated correctly a removal request is put to the gateway DIRAC instance to be relayed to the RunDB.
Bulk Data Replication

Once moved to CASTOR the RAW physics data is Grid visible and can be replicated using standard Grid tools. The DIRAC bulk replication framework is built on a central repository of replication requests (TransferDB) which aggregates individual requests into bulk transfer jobs (see Figure 5). These bulk transfer jobs are retrieved from the TransferDB by a Transfer Agent and submitted to the gLite File Transfer Service [7] which provides reliable transfer over dedicated Optical Private Networks between the Tier-1 centers. The bulk transfer framework architecture has been defined by an iterative process building on experience. The previous solution was a distributed transfer management system which used the LHCb VO boxes, present on the Tier-1 centers, as request repositories. These requests were executed individually by agents present on the VO boxes. This architecture ensures the persistency of data management requests; each VO box is identical so clients can place their requests on any available VO box, ensuring the redundancy of the service. The disadvantage of this approach was that transfer agents on the VO boxes would throttle the requests under their management, but had no knowledge of other agent requests. The load placed on the SEs with this system proved unpredictable and resulted in degraded global performance. The current solution uses a centralized repository, allowing the optimization of resources and intelligent scheduling,  with distributed failover mechanism (discussed in more detail in [8]). The distributed failover mechanism ensures the persistency of the requests if the central repository is unavailable.
Resource Optimization

When replicating data it is essential that the data be available on disk. Waiting for the file to be recalled from tape, within the transfer operation results in a waste of resources. The architecture of FTS is such that transfer slots, waiting for files to become available, simply timeout, resulting in severe throughput penalty. This problem is resolved using the DIRAC Stager service [8] [9]. When scheduling the transfer, the locality of the file on tape or disk storage is determined from the replica catalogue entry. If residing on tape storage a request is put to the Stager. These requests are then executed by an agent, contacting the SRM [10] [11] services of the SEs requesting files be pre-staged. The agent then polls the SRM for the status of the request and informs the TransferDB when the file is available on disk. The file is then available to be replicated. This system is illustrated in Figure 6.
Intelligent Scheduling

At Petabyte scale Grid computing the optimal use of network resources is important. The FTS, designed as a reliable point to point transfer system, does not perform any advanced scheduling. The FTS architecture is based on logical channels that reflect the high bandwidth OPN at the fabric level. Each logical channel is configured to execute a certain number of transfers concurrently, which is used by site managers to reduce or increase transfer load. With limited concurrent transfers on each channel a 'task queue' of files waiting to transfer will develop at saturation point. To make optimal use of the network resource, intelligent scheduling can be performed, which schedules replication paths based on the current state of the 'task queues' and channel throughput. For example, the channel defined from A to B may have a high 'time to start' (many files in the task queue and/or low observed throughput) while the task queues linking A to C and C to B may be more performant. If a file is to be replicated from site A to sites B and C and the combined 'time to start' of the A-C-B route is lower than that of the direct A-B route, it is more efficient to schedule the replication first from A to C, then from C to B. To do this, 'task queues' are maintained in the TransferDB which reflect the underlying FTS channels. The observed bandwidth (not necessarily the actual throughput) of the channel along with the number and size of the files in the queue is maintained. At the point of transfer scheduling the 'Replication Optimizer' evaluates the 'weight' of the available routes to determine the most optimal replication path. It then populates the task queues accordingly (see Figure 7).  Figure 7. Population of the Task Queue by Replication Optimizer
Data Driven Production Management

The dataflow in the LHCb Computing Model requires an interaction between the Data Management and Workload Management Systems. Each System has a component into which data must be registered for automated action to take place; for Workload Management the ProcessingDB and Data Management the AutoDataTransferDB. These components offer the standard DIRAC File Catalogue API, such that addition may be made transparently at the point of file catalogue registration. Registration is all that is required by a client to trigger processing or replication as the data becomes available. The ProcessingDB and AutoDataTransferDB have associated agents that manipulate the contents of the database. The Transformation Agent queries the ProcessingDB to find candidate files for processing activities, also defined in the DB. Jobs for matching files are created by the agent and submitted to the WMS for execution, as illustrated in Figure 8 (see [1] for more details). Analogously, the AutoDataTransferDB is queried by the Replication Agent which checks for files matching replication operations stored in the DB. Files matching the operations defined are wrapped in a replication request and placed in the TransferDB for execution (see Figure 5). The logic of the Replication Agent support multiple operation types including single source to multiple destinations and splitting groups of files based on a configurable share, although other operations types may be plugged-in.
RAW Data

To trigger the full chain of the LHCb dataflow the RAW data must be registered in the AutoDataTransferDB. As detailed in Section 3.2 the Online Integrity Agent ensures that the file migrated to tape by CASTOR has not been corrupted. Once this check is successfully performed the Online Integrity Agent registers the file in the LCG File Catalogue [12] (LHCb's baseline replica catalogue) and the AutoDataTransferDB as shown in Figure 9. To meet the needs of the Computing Model the Replication Agent is configured with a replication operation to split the RAW data to match the amount of the Tier-1 center pledged computing resources. This mechanism was tested during the Data Challenge 2006 exercise [13] and showed performance in excess of the 40MB/s export rate required to support the Computing Model (see Figure 10). Processing of the RAW data is triggered with registration of the replicated data in the ProcessingDB.
DST Data

As stated in Section 2 the processing activities at the Tier-1 centers produce DST files. For DST files produced from real physics data these must be replicated to all Tier-1 centers for load balanced distributed user analysis. The DST files produced from simulated physics data must be present on selected Tier-1 centers only. There are two possible mechanisms for distributing these DST files. The first is by giving the output sites to the jobs in the workflow such the destinations for the files are known on the worker node. The job places replication requests directly from the worker node to the TransferDB (as shown in Figure 5). The above mechanism is sufficient for DST files produced from real data but, for DST files produced from simulated data, the destination for the output data is not known on the worker node. The distribution of these DST files in a load balanced way can be achieved using the mechanism employed for the replication of RAW files. In this case the job would register the file in the AutoDataTransferDB after uploading to the Tier-1 center storage (as shown in Figure  11). The final destinations of this output data may then be determined by the Replication Agent according to a defined share. The replication requests would then be placed in the TransferDB for execution. This mechanism could be employed for the distribution of real data, where the replication operation is defined with all sites as the destination. During the WLCG 'Dress Rehearsal' exercise the performance of both strategies will be evaluated and the decision on which mechanism to use for real data will be made.
Conclusions

In this paper DIRAC has been shown to fully support the LHCb Computing Model. The throughput required during the upload of data from the Online System to CASTOR has been demonstrated and surpassed. The bulk data transfer architecture of a centralized repository with distributed failover mechanism has proven to be scalable to the throughput required. The mechanisms for optimizing resource usage and performing intelligent scheduling were presented. Most importantly, DIRAC has demonstrated the ability to perform 'data-driven' production management involving the coordination of the Workload and Data Management Systems. This coordination allows the execution of the LHCb dataflow and is flexible enough to support a variety of use cases.
